transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-09-14 16:30 PST
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE); Maya Ortega (Redwood SE); Liam Patel (Redwood Solutions Eng); Dr. Elena Park (CTO, Peregrine); Marcus Hale (VP Eng); Priya Ramesh (Security & Compliance); Tom Ruiz (Infra Lead); Ana Morales (QA)

Auto-summary (auto):
- Customer evaluating private on-prem air-gapped deployment for imaging inference workload.
- Key constraints: no outbound network, signed removable media for updates, constrained chassis (2x A100s per rack node), NVMe capacity limited, strict audit and KMS handling.
- Next: security pack + on-site workshop + offline benchmark.

Topics:
- Deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
- Offline update/rotation process and signing
- Hardware constraints and model footprint/quantization
- Audit logs, KMS/HSM integration, SSO/SAML concerns
- Pilot scope and timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Jordan Kim from Redwood, I'll hand it to Maya for the technical overview but first quick intros?
[00:10] Dr. Elena Park: Elena here, CTO at Peregrine imaging. We run a mixed fleet of inference for radiology post-processing, lots of patient PHI, so everything needs to be inside our data center.
[00:22] Marcus: Marcus, VP Eng. We're looking at options to move from ad-hoc models to a supported inference platform, goal is stable latency and predictable cost.
[00:30] Priya: Priya, security and compliance. We need auditability, full key control — no external KMS unless through our HSM connectors, and signed update process.
[00:38] Tom: Tom, infra. We have 3 racks with dual-GPU nodes, mostly A100-ish class but some older 80GB cards and a couple of RTX6000s. Storage is tight, about 8TB usable per node after redundancy.
[00:50] Jordan: Great, thanks. Maya do you want to take us through how Redwood handles private/offline deployments?
[00:56] Maya: Sure. So Redwood Private — uh, sorry sometimes the transcript says Red...Redwood Privacy — essentially we provide a control plane that can sit in a separate network or be fully air gapped. For air-gapped we package signed artifacts: models, runtime, and a deployment bundle that you can transfer via removable media. The customer retains the private keys in their HSM; we never push secrets.
[01:20] Tom: Quick question — what does the signed artifact look like? Is it a tarball with signatures or a container image?
[01:26] Maya: It's typically a signed tarball with metadata including manifest, hash, and signature (we support RSA-PSS and also a YubiHSM signing flow). For customers that want FIPS-approved signatures we provide the manifest format and verification tool. A note — some of our early notes call the manifest a "map file" which confuses people, so we call it manifest now.
[01:44] Priya: How do you handle key rotation? We need periodic key rotation without exposing old images to outside networks.
[01:51] Maya: We support offline key rotation workflows: you generate a new key in your HSM, sign the next bundle offline, and then perform a chain-of-trust rollover that the local runtime validates. The runtime keeps a small key vault that stores the public verification keys; rotation is atomic during a maintenance window.
[02:06] Marcus: Our ops team needs specifics around rollback. If an update fails mid-apply, can the node automatically revert to previous model/runtime without network?
[02:14] Maya: Yes, the runtime maintains N previous good artifacts (configurable, default 2). It validates signatures and runs a preflight smoke test locally; if the smoke test fails the system reverts to the previous artifact. The preflight includes a small inference pass using a canned sample.
[02:30] Ana: Is the canned sample a patient data simulant or synthetic? We can't store PHI.
[02:35] Maya: It's synthetic, we ship test vectors that are non-PHI.
[02:38] Tom: On hardware — our NVMe is low, so we can't store multiple large model variants. Can Redwood run a quantized model or support dynamic swapping from a network share inside the air-gapped site?
[02:52] Liam: Jumping in — we often recommend model quantization (INT8 or 4-bit) if you need to fit multiple variants. Redwood Optimize can produce quantized builds and we also support on-the-fly loading of KV cache to reduce memory. Note: 4-bit can give big size wins but requires perf validation.
[03:09] Marcus: If we go 4-bit, what's the perf hit on latency? For inference on 2k token-ish medical notes, we need sub-200ms p95.
[03:19] Maya: It depends on model architecture — for large decoder-only models you'll see some latency savings with INT8 using tensorized kernels; with 4-bit it's model and hardware dependent. We can run a quick batch of benchmarks on your sample traces to show token throughput and p95.
[03:36] Priya: Audit logs — we need immutable logs of who applied updates, change hashes, and operator identity. We also require tamper-evident chain of custody for media that transfers artifacts.
[03:49] Jordan: We can provide an audit subsystem that writes signed audit events to the local log and an append-only ledger file; operators sign the apply action with their key. For chain of custody we recommend a manifest that is printed and sealed with a physical signature when media leaves staging.
[04:08] Dr. Elena Park: The physical process is a big deal for us. Our current SOP is: staging in secure room -> checksum printed -> sealed courier -> onsite verification. Will Redwood fit into that?
[04:20] Maya: Yes, that fits. Customers usually adopt our signing tool in staging and we provide the verification tool on the target nodes.
[04:26] Tom: What about firmware and driver updates? Sometimes vendors push CUDA and driver updates that break runtimes. We can't accept external outbound checks.
[04:37] Liam: We recommend a staged test lab node where driver/firmware combos are validated using Redwood's runtime compatibility matrix. We produce an upgrade matrix with known good combos. In practice we avoid forcing driver updates in the bundle unless absolutely necessary.
[04:53] Marcus: Pricing question — how is Private priced versus Dedicated? We're doing ROI calculations.
[04:59] Jordan: Private has a platform fee plus per-node license and support. Dedicated is reserved capacity in our cloud hardware — typically lower up-front but you accept external hosting. We can share a line-item pricing sheet after the call.
[05:11] Priya: On SSO — we have SAML SSO internally. Will Redwood runtime communicate with our IdP?
[05:18] Maya: The control plane in an air-gapped setup doesn't talk to external IdP. For operator authentication we support local RBAC mapped to exported SAML assertions consumed via a JWT-minting step you run in your staging environment. Basically you mint a signed short-lived token that the node uses to map to local roles.
[05:36] Tom: Are telemetry/metrics optional? We cannot allow telemetry to leave the site.
[05:40] Maya: Telemetry is optional and can be fully disabled. Alternatively we support a push model where metrics are exported to an internal monitoring endpoint you control; nothing goes out unless you configure it.
[05:50] Dr. Elena Park: What about model provenance and model cataloging — we need immutable metadata for which model version served which patient case.
[05:59] Jordan: Each request logs model-id, artifact-hash, and runtime-version. The audit log ties to the operator session. We can also add a policy binding to record which model was pinned per route.
[06:12] Marcus: On the hardware side, we have a mixture of PCIe lane counts and older power supplies. Any particular constraints for your runtime?
[06:19] Maya: The runtime is somewhat flexible but we do require contiguous GPU memory for certain kernels. If you run older cards with limited BAR sizes we may fall back to alternate kernels with slightly higher CPU usage. We'll evaluate during the inventory.
[06:35] Priya: Regulatory — we need to show evidence of data residency and encryption both at rest and in transit (even internal). Do you support FIPS 140-2 for crypto modules?
[06:46] Liam: We support FIPS-alg compatible stacks when customers request them and integrate with customer HSMs for key material. The verification tooling can be run in your secure lab and we provide test vectors.
[06:55] Ana: For QA we'll run replays of live traffic. How do you recommend capturing synthetic traces that match production?
[07:02] Maya: We'll share a trace-capture guide; best practice is to strip PHI client-side, synthesize identifiers, and provide sample distribution of sequence lengths. We'll also ask for p95/p99 targets for latency.
[07:15] Marcus: Timeline — we're hoping for a pilot in Q4. Is that realistic?
[07:20] Jordan: Yes, pilot in Q4 is realistic: week-long bench and a 4-node pilot cluster is typical. Steps: inventory -> security checklist -> signed bundle test -> bench -> pilot -> canary.
[07:30] Priya: Who are typical internal stakeholders we should plan for? We have legal and procurement; they usually ask for SOC2, ISO docs and proof of penetration test.
[07:40] Jordan: We'll send the SOC2 summary and our penetration test summary. We also have a red-team report redacted for customer distribution.
[07:51] Tom: One more — offline telemetry for debugging: can operators dump traces to a USB then we analyze them offsite?
[07:57] Maya: Yes, we provide an offline trace collector. It produces an encrypted bundle that you can forward to Redwood if you want, but only if you choose to. The bundle itself is encrypted with your public key.
[08:10] Dr. Elena Park: Let's drill into the practical update window. Our radiology clinic has a 2AM-4AM maintenance window. Can the bundle be applied in that window safely across 30 nodes?
[08:20] Maya: Mostly yes; rollout orchestration supports staged apply with an operator-controlled concurrency. For 30 nodes you'll want a canary set of 2-3 nodes, then a staggered wave. The entire apply usually completes within the window depending on model size. If model count is large we recommend pre-loading artifacts overnight.
[08:38] Marcus: Pre-loading is tricky given NVMe constraints. Can we pre-load to a central air-gapped cache server and then copy locally during the window?
[08:46] Liam: Yes, an internal cache/gateway is a common pattern — you store artifacts on an internal file server and use verified rsync or block-copy during the window. The local verifier checks signatures post-copy.
[08:58] Ana: What about signatures being stripped in copy? We need end-to-end checksum validation.
[09:03] Maya: The verifier checks both the manifest hash and the signature and will reject any artifact where either doesn't match.
[09:09] Jordan: Quick note: we sometimes see customers try to save space by compressing artifacts; that's fine but you must preserve the manifest hash discipline.
[09:17] Marcus: Security aside, who at Redwood will be our primary contact during pilot?
[09:21] Jordan: I'll be the AE for commercial and coordination, Maya will be the technical lead, and Liam will handle the operations integration.
[09:29] Priya: Can you walk us through a sample chain-of-custody for media?
[09:34] Maya: Sure. Staging: build artifact -> sign with customer HSM -> print manifest and QR -> seal in tamper-evident bag -> courier manifest receipt signed -> on arrival operator scans QR and runs verification tool. The verification tool outputs audit entries to the local ledger and requires operator signature to proceed.
[09:56] Tom: About driver compatibility again — if we have a kernel update requirement, how do you recommend we manage vendor-signed kernels in air-gapped mode?
[10:05] Liam: Keep a vendor staging node that gets driver/firmware updates and is used strictly for validation. Do not push to production nodes until verified. Version-lock kernel packages and document the minimum supported versions in the compatibility matrix.
[10:18] Marcus: Any gotchas you see commonly?
[10:21] Maya: Two big ones: 1) not planning for rollback storage — if you can't store previous artifacts you'll lose the safety net; 2) underestimating the size of model KV caches which can blow up memory.
[10:34] Dr. Elena Park: How do you measure KV cache growth?
[10:38] Maya: We instrument generation heatmaps and can simulate worst-case conversational traces. For imaging post-processing workloads the KV usage depends on the sequence length — usually smaller than chat workloads but depends on model context window.
[10:52] Marcus: Let's talk about legal/procurement. What's typical SLA for Private customers?
[10:58] Jordan: Private SLAs are tailored; standard offering is 99.9% platform availability for supported configuration plus response SLAs for critical incidents. We include a support runbook and optional 24/7 support.
[11:10] Priya: For compliance we need data deletion proofs and retention policy support.
[11:14] Liam: We support retention tagging and deletion workflows; deletion actions are logged and can produce attestations. We can coordinate a runbook for HIPAA-ready deletion processes.
[11:26] Ana: For QA acceptance, what are exit criteria from pilot?
[11:29] Maya: Usually: p95 latency within agreed SLO, successful offline update cycle demonstrated, audit/event logs accessible, and integration with your operator workflows.
[11:39] Marcus: Anything else from your side, Elena?
[11:41] Dr. Elena Park: No, but I want the security pack and the benchmark ask list by next week so we can align internal stakeholders.
[11:48] Jordan: Copy that. We'll send security pack and a checklist. Also we'll include a sample canary plan and a template for the custody manifest.
[11:58] Marcus: Also please include an approximate TCO model for Private vs Dedicated so procurement can see numbers.
[12:05] Jordan: Will do.
[12:08] Priya: On the vendor side — you mentioned YubiHSM earlier. We use nCipher HSMs in our data center. Any issues?
[12:16] Maya: We integrate with PKCS#11-compatible HSMs so nCipher should be fine; we'll capture exact endpoints during inventory.
[12:23] Tom: Final question — if we need to air-gap a small subset of nodes while keeping others connected for analytics, is hybrid supported?
[12:30] Liam: Yes, hybrid topologies are common: some nodes can be private while others route telemetry to a regional Redwood Dedicated cluster. Routing policies are configurable.
[12:40] Jordan: Ok, quick recap of next steps and owners: Jordan to send security pack and pricing; Maya to send benchmark ask list and offline update checklist; Tom to provide hardware inventory; customer to propose dates for on-site workshop. Anything to add?
[12:55] Dr. Elena Park: That's it, thanks everyone.
[13:00] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up by EOD tomorrow with links.

End of transcript.
